title: Social care means Bristol City Council faces £15m black hole
excerpt: The budget gap in Bristol could reach a whopping £67.5 million in five years' time
content:
Rising demand for costly social care means Bristol City Council facing £15m black hole

The budget gap in Bristol could reach a whopping £67.5 million in five years' time

14:00, 15 Oct 2026

Rising demand for costly social care means that Bristol City Council is forecast to spend £15 million over its budget this year. The council is now consulting the public on potential changes to local services, as well as once again raising council tax by five per cent next April.

‌

‌

Over the next five years the council’s budget deficit is predicted to get worse, with a budget gap of £26 million next year, and then reaching £67.5 million by 2031. Inflation and the cost of living are also contributing to the problem, with supplies now more expensive and wages increasing.

‌

Next year’s budget consultation runs until November 25 and can be completed on the council’s website. An update on the council’s budget was given to the strategy and resources policy committee on Monday, October 12.

‌

Labour Councillor Tom Blenkinsop said: “We’re getting an incredible financial risk with regards to children in care. There’s always been a lot of concern about out-of-area placements. That is and remains one of our key problems financially.”

He added that the Labour government has provided a lot more money to councils than previous Conservative governments, including potentially writing off almost £100 million of a deficit built up from high spending on special educational needs and disabilities. However Green councillors insisted that “austerity hasn’t ended” and there was still too little money for local services.

‌

Green Cllr Heather Mack, deputy council leader, added: “We don’t have the money to cover the services that we want to deliver. We know there’s a massive high cost to children’s out-of-area placements. It’s not a case that we can, in any way, stop that. It would be illegal, it would be cruel.

“Unfortunately we know these costs are coming and are going to keep coming and we’re going to do a lot of preventative work. The money that is coming from the government for local authority spending still does not add up. Austerity hasn’t ended in terms of the funding that we have for the local authority and the services that we want.”

‌

Last month Andy Burnham, the prime minister, revealed plans for a new National Care Service. However there are few details of these plans so far, and previous governments have repeatedly tried and failed to reform the social care system, while the population is getting older and sicker.

Sarah Chodkiewicz, finance director, said: “At this stage it’s extremely difficult to even hazard a guess until we know much more about what that will look like and how that’s going to be funded, what the structure and format of that is, and what the breadth and scale of it is.”

‌

After the meeting, Green Cllr Tony Dyer, leader of the council, said that despite the financial pressures facing local government, the council is still investing in services like housing, support for children and families, and communities. He missed the committee meeting, which he usually chairs, as he was in Geneva attending a United Nations event preceded by a cocktail reception.

Cllr Dyer added: “In the coming weeks, residents will have the opportunity to help shape next year’s budget through our annual public consultation. We will be seeking views on council tax and a range of proposals intended to help close the financial gap we face.

“These conversations are never easy. Every pound spent in one area is a pound unavailable elsewhere, and we know residents are facing financial pressures of their own. But it is important that people understand both the challenges we face and the choices ahead.”
